tagline.text: A cliffside waterfall at the end of a gorge, reached by paddling upriver through rapids

children.text: Manila's most famous waterfall day trip: you ride a wooden bangka steered by two boatmen up the rapids of a narrow gorge to a waterfall pouring from a cliff about
high, and on into the cave behind it.

Pagsanjan Falls is a three-tiered waterfall that drops from the Cavinti highlands of Laguna Province into the Pagsanjan River; its official name is Cavinti Falls, and locals call it Magdapio Falls. Its height is most often given as about
(300 feet), though some sources put the longest drop at about

. The deep pool beneath the falls and the cave behind the curtain of water (commonly called the Devil's Cave) are especially famous. It has long been one of the Philippines' signature natural attractions, declared a national park as early as

What makes this place special is less the waterfall itself than the journey to reach it. From the riverbank in Pagsanjan town, you board a narrow wooden bangka paddled by two boatmen (bangkeros), one at the bow and one at the stern, and travel upriver through a gorge flanked by moss-covered cliffs dozens of meters high. At the swiftest rapids, the boatmen climb out onto the rocks and push and haul the boat up by hand — a practice called "Shooting the Rapids" that dates back to the Spanish colonial era, with records of it going back to
. Part of the river scenes in the film "Apocalypse Now" are also said to have been shot in this area.

Once you reach the falls, you switch to a bamboo raft and ride straight into the cave, taking the full force of the falling water. On the way back, you shoot down the same rapids you struggled up earlier, adding an extra thrill. The facilities are modest given the site's long-standing fame, and there's a tipping culture to be aware of, but few places within
2–3 hours
of Manila offer gorge scenery like this.

It suits family trips, trips with parents in tow, and business travelers in Manila who want to carve out a day to see nature. The physical demands are minimal, so children and older travelers can comfortably enjoy the bangka ride, and those wanting something more active can take the trekking route down the stairs from the Cavinti side.

The falls have three tiers. The uppermost, Naculo Falls, can only be seen from the park viewpoint on the Cavinti side; the middle tier is hidden by the gorge; and the bangkas reach the main falls at the bottom. The boat route from Pagsanjan town to the falls is about
5km
, and along the way several thin streams, including Talahib Falls, hang from the cliffs, though most of them dry up in the dry season.
of the gorge area is protected as Pagsanjan Gorge National Park, and it was also declared a tourist zone in
. There's also a well-known story about a Pagsanjan Falls stamp issued in
, during the American colonial period, that mistakenly depicted Vernal Fall in Yosemite in the United States and was withdrawn within six months.
Setting out from a riverside resort or the official dock in Pagsanjan, you travel upriver through the gorge for about
1–1.5 hours
. You can watch up close as the boatmen push and haul the boat over some 14 rapids.

blocks.title: Raft trip into the cave behind the falls

children.text: At the pool in front of the falls, switch to a bamboo raft and pass beneath the water curtain into the cave. The water pressure is considerable, so wear a helmet and keep your belongings in a waterproof bag.
The return trip rides the current down at a completely different pace from the climb up. The further forward you sit, the more water you'll get splashed with.

Several thin ribbons of waterfall stream down the cliffs on both sides. The moss and water look most vivid when the slanting morning sunlight reaches in. At the rest stop in front of Talahib Falls, midway along the route, the boatmen catch their breath and vendors sell drinks and snacks. On days when the water is high, the bangkas sometimes go only as far as Talahib Falls before turning back.

A way to reach the falls by descending several hundred metal steps from Pueblo El Salvador Nature Park in Cavinti. Some sections involve rope descents and raft crossings, offering a different kind of adventure from the bangka ride.

blocks.title: Cavinti underground river and cave complex

children.text: On the Cavinti side, tours exploring an underground river and caves also run, so you can combine them with the falls for a full-day itinerary. The caves are near the villages of Mahipon and Paowin in Cavinti, and nearby Lake Caliraya and Lake Lumot are man-made reservoirs built for hydroelectric power, lined with lakeside resorts for kayaking and fishing.
The town still has Our Lady of Guadalupe Church, founded in the 17th century, and the Pagsanjan Arch, construction of which began in
, making it a good place for a short look around. The parish was established in
; the church was destroyed by bombing in
and later rebuilt, and the arch, with its three stone gateways, has been designated national cultural heritage. Pagsanjan was the capital of Laguna Province between
, so old houses still line Rizal Street.
On the way back, be sure to try Laguna's famous buko pie (coconut pie) and kesong puti, a soft white cheese made from carabao milk.

The Pueblo El Salvador route takes about
1 hour
going down and about
2 hours

coming back up because of the vertical ladders and metal stairs. Only those aged 12–59 can take part, and it closes in bad weather, so check with the Cavinti tourism office the day before to confirm it's open.

items.subtitle: Getting there and back by bus and jeepney

children.text: Board a DLTB or JAC Liner bus to Santa Cruz at Buendia in Pasay (or at PITX/Cubao)
Get off at Pagsawitan, on the border of Santa Cruz and Pagsanjan, and transfer to a jeepney bound for Pagsanjan town
Register at the Pagsanjan tourist information office or the official dock, pay the fee in cash, and get a life vest and helmet
Bangka departs — on the calm lower stretch, a motorboat tows a line of bangkas, and from the gorge onward the boatmen paddle and push the boat
Short break at the rest stop in front of Talahib Falls
Arrive at the main falls, pass beneath the falling water on a bamboo raft and explore the cave
Shoot the rapids downstream for about
45 minutes
, and hand the boatmen a tip before getting off at the dock
Shower and change, then lunch in town (for example at Calle Arco, a restaurant in a restored old house)
Stroll around Our Lady of Guadalupe Church and the Pagsanjan Arch, then try halo-halo at Aling Taleng's
Take a jeepney to the Pagsawitan or Santa Cruz terminal and board a bus to Manila
Arrive in Manila (it takes longer on Friday and Sunday afternoons due to SLEX traffic)
Bangkas usually leave sometime between
8 AM and 3 PM
, and after heavy rain, whether boats will run is decided that morning. The round trip plus time at the falls takes around
3 hours
, so it's best to board before noon at the latest.
From Manila, take SLEX to the Calamba exit, then pass through Los Baños, Bay, and Santa Cruz to reach Pagsanjan. It's about
100km
, taking
2–3 hours
depending on traffic. Toll costs are about
one way. Most riverside resorts have parking.

If you're setting out from the east side of Metro Manila, such as Quezon City or Pasig, you can also reach Pagsanjan via Manila East Road, which passes through Taytay and Tanay in Rizal Province and then runs down past the towns on the eastern shore of Laguna Lake (Siniloan, Paete, and Lumban). The road is narrow with many curves, but it lets you avoid SLEX traffic. From the main junction in the center of Pagsanjan town, cross the Balanac Bridge and take the mountain road up to the right to head toward Cavinti.
In Manila, take a bus bound for Santa Cruz (Sta. Cruz, Laguna) from Buendia (Pasay), Cubao, PITX, or Alabang. DLTB and JAC Liner leave Buendia about every
30 minutes
, and HM Transport departs from Cubao and Alabang. The trip takes about
2.5–3.5 hours
and costs about
HM Transport and LLI buses stop at the Pagsawitan terminal on the border of Santa Cruz and Pagsanjan, close to Pagsanjan town. From Santa Cruz or Pagsawitan to Pagsanjan town is about
10–15 minutes
by jeepney at about
per person, and chartering a tricycle to the dock costs about
Touts around the bus terminals often push overpriced bangka rides, so it's best to go directly to the Pagsanjan tourist information office or the official dock.
Bus and jeepney fares went up from
September 28, 2026
due to rising fuel costs, so check the fare when you buy your ticket. The last bus from Santa Cruz to Manila usually leaves around
8–9 PM
Day tours with hotel pickup in Manila sell for about

per person (varying with joined tour or private vehicle, and whether lunch is included). If your group is small or you'd rather not drive, a tour can actually be the more economical choice. Boatmen's tips are usually not included in the tour price, so you pay them separately in cash.
The Cavinti trekking route requires about
30 minutes
up a mountain road from Pagsanjan town by tricycle or jeepney. Public transport is scarce, so it's more convenient to charter a vehicle.

To reach the Cavinti side by public transport, take a jeepney bound for Cavinti from Santa Cruz, get off at the Magdapio Falls junction, and take a tricycle to the entrance of Pueblo El Salvador park.

From Lucban or Lucena in Quezon Province, take a jeepney from Lucban that runs via Luisiana and Cavinti to Santa Cruz; it passes through Cavinti and then Pagsanjan. From the Rizal Province side, take a jeepney bound for Santa Cruz from Siniloan, ride past the towns on the eastern shore of Laguna Lake, and get off at Pagsanjan. On the way from
Lucban
, the road runs past one mountain village after another at the foot of Mount Banahaw.
Water levels at the falls are abundant during the wet season (
June–November
) and noticeably lower toward the end of the dry season (
April–May
). The best recommended time is from late in the wet season into early dry season,
October–January
, when there's still plenty of water without the river running too high.
Right after a typhoon or during prolonged heavy rain, the river can rise sharply and bangka operations are suspended.
July–October
sees frequent typhoons, so it's safer to call ahead the day before to check whether boats are running. Conversely, during the
March–May
dry season the weather is clear but the rapids run shallow, lengthening the stretches where boatmen must haul the boat, and the falls themselves run thinner.

Inside the gorge it stays shaded even at midday, so it feels cooler than in town, but the sun is strong while you wait for a bangka, so bring a hat and sunscreen. Lines for bangkas get long on weekends and during Holy Week (Easter week), so a weekday morning visit is recommended.
Daytime temperatures in town are coolest in
January–February
, at about
, and rise to about
in
April–May
. Pagsanjan's Bangkero Festival, with boatmen's canoe races and street parades, is usually held in
April
(in
it was cut to a single day,
April 25
, as a fuel-saving measure), and
December 12
is the feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe, Pagsanjan's patron saint. Neighboring Cavinti holds the Sambalilo hat festival in
early August
, and Lumban holds its embroidery festival in the
third week of September

Most visitors come and go the same day, but if you want to catch the first bangka early in the morning or combine this with a wider trip around Laguna, staying overnight at a Pagsanjan riverside resort is a good option. Riverside resorts run about
a night, and many of them also serve as bangka departure points, which is convenient. For a more comfortable stay, San Pablo or the hot spring resorts around Calamba and Los Baños, about
30–40 minutes
away by car, are another option.

Laguna's signature food is buko pie. A row of buko pie shops lines the highway through Los Baños, making it easy to pick some up on your way back. You can also commonly find white cheese kesong puti made from carabao milk, rice cakes called kalamay, and dishes made from tilapia and freshwater shrimp caught in Laguna Lake. The neighboring towns of Santa Cruz and Lumban, next to Pagsanjan, are also known for their traditional embroidery workshops that weave pineapple-fiber fabric into barong tagalog, worth a stop if you're shopping for souvenirs. Lumban embroidery ranges from small items like handkerchiefs and table runners to formal wear costing tens of thousands of pesos. Filipino-style barbecue and sinigang (sour soup) at the riverside restaurants are perfect for warming up after getting soaked on the bangka.

If you're eating in Pagsanjan town, Calle Arco on Rizal Street is known as a restaurant in a restored old house. In rooms decorated with antiques, it serves Laguna-style home cooking such as beef sinigang with jackfruit for about
per person. Across the Balanac Bridge in Maulawin, Aling Taleng's has been making halo-halo since
, and its specialty is old-fashioned halo-halo piled high with coconut-based toppings. For buko pie, The Original Buko Pie, founded in
, and Lety's, founded in

, stand side by side on the highway in Los Baños, convenient for picking some up on the way back. In town there are also small lodgings that can arrange falls tours for you, such as Casa Marina, a B&B in a restored old mansion.

Book your bangka only through the Pagsanjan tourist information office, the official dock, or a registered resort, and get a receipt. Touts who approach you on the street commonly charge two or three times the official rate.
A single bangka usually carries 2–3 passengers. The boatmen assign seats based on weight distribution, so it's safest to follow their instructions.
Assume your clothes will get completely soaked, and wear quick-dry clothing along with aqua shoes or sandals. Leave a change of clothes and a towel in the car or at the resort.
Keep your phone and camera in a waterproof pouch worn around your neck. The current is strong during the cave experience, so anything held in your hands is easy to lose.
The best time to go is a weekday departure at
8–9 AM
. There are fewer people, and the sunlight coming into the gorge makes for great photos.
Cash is the standard way to pay on site. There are ATMs in Pagsanjan town, but they can run out of cash on weekends, so bring enough from Manila.
Some boatmen ask for a tip on the way back. Check what's included in the fare before you set off, and offer a tip just before disembarking, based on how satisfied you were with the service.
The Cavinti trekking route has steep, slippery stairs, so bring gloves and sturdy-soled shoes.

Bangka fares are posted per person, but if you use a whole boat by yourself you may be asked for an extra charge. If you're traveling solo, ask at the dock whether you can share a boat with other travelers.
The Pueblo El Salvador route in Cavinti costs about

per person including the entrance fee, guide, harness, helmet, and life vest, but because it's physically demanding, only those aged 12–59 are accepted. If you're traveling with children or your parents, choose the bangka ride on the Pagsanjan side.
Never board a bangka right after heavy rain or when there's a typhoon warning in effect. The river in the gorge can rise sharply within a few hours.
Life vests and helmets are mandatory, not optional. You'll pass close to rocks at the rapids, so don't put your hands out over the side of the boat.
If a passenger stands up or moves seats while the boatmen are pushing and hauling the boat, it can capsize. Don't lean far out to take photos.
There are no restrooms inside the gorge, so take care of that before you set off. The rest area in front of the falls is very basic.

If you're asked for extra charges on top of the official fare, such as a "fuel fee" or "cave raft fee," double-check what's included, and report it to the tourist information office if there's a problem.
The water pressure during the cave experience can make it feel hard to breathe. If you have a heart condition or are afraid of water, feel free to skip the raft experience.
The Pagsanjan Arch stands in the middle of a national highway with constant traffic. When taking photos, don't step into the road; shoot from the sidewalks on either side.
About
1 hour
by car. A coconut plantation resort where you have lunch at tables right below a waterfall.
About
40 minutes
by car. A cluster of seven volcanic crater lakes, where a walk around Lake Sampaloc is worthwhile.
About
1 hour

About
1 hour
